name: Major depressive disorder
summary: Major depressive disorder has dozens of FDA-approved antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, bupropion, mirtazapine, vortioxetine, vilazodone, gepirone, dextromethorphan-bupropion, TCAs, MAOIs). Five atypical antipsychotics are approved as adjuncts (aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, quetiapine XR, cariprazine, and lumateperone since 11/2025). Esketamine nasal spray (TRD, monotherapy since 01/2025; and MDD with acute suicidal ideation) and olanzapine-fluoxetine (TRD) cover more resistant illness. Every antidepressant carries the boxed warning on suicidal thoughts and behaviors in young people; as of 10/2026 that warning is unchanged and no pregnancy boxed warning has been added.
plainSummary: Major depression is a common, treatable illness with persistent low mood or loss of interest that affects daily life. Many medicines are approved to treat it, and others can be added or switched to if the first one does not work well enough.
sections: Depressive symptoms with acute suicidal ideation

approved.indication: Treatment of major depressive disorder (MDD) in adults (Effexor XR capsules; venlafaxine IR tablets and ER tablets also carry MDD labeling).

dosing.start: ER: 75 mg once daily (37.5 mg for 4–7 days in some patients); IR: 75 mg/day in 2–3 divided doses

Hepatic impairment: reduce 50% (more in cirrhosis). The 112.5 mg-only venlafaxine ER tablet (besylate) must not be used for initiation or titration. Taper on discontinuation. Effexor XR approved 1997.

approved.indication: Treatment of major depressive disorder (MDD), as defined by the DSM, with bupropion products labeled for depression (IR/SR/XL HCl and XL HBr). Smoking-cessation-only SR products are not indicated for depression.

dosing.start: IR: 100 mg twice daily; SR: 150 mg once daily; XL: 150 mg once daily; Aplenzin (HBr): 174 mg once daily
dosing.target: 300 mg/day (IR 100 mg three times daily; SR 150 mg twice daily; XL 300 mg once daily; Aplenzin 348 mg)
dosing.max: IR: 450 mg/day (no single dose >150 mg); SR: 400 mg/day; XL: 450 mg/day; Aplenzin: 522 mg/day
dosing.notes: Titrate gradually to reduce seizure risk (dose-related). Forfivo XL (450 mg only) cannot be used to start therapy; use after at least 2 weeks at 300 mg/day of another formulation. Moderate–severe hepatic impairment: e.g., XL 150 mg every other day, SR 100 mg/day or 150 mg every other day. Consider dose reduction in renal impairment. Wellbutrin IR approved 1985 (marketed 1989).

contraindications: SSRIs, SNRIs, clomipramine, imipramine, meperidine, tramadol, methadone, pentazocine, propoxyphene, dextromethorphan
approved.plainSummary: A skin-patch MAOI antidepressant for adults. At the lowest dose no special diet is needed, but higher doses need a low-tyramine diet.

source.label: Emsam (selegiline transdermal system) prescribing information, DailyMed

approved.indication: Adjunctive treatment of major depressive disorder (adults already taking an antidepressant).

dosing.notes: Adjust by up to 5 mg/day at intervals of at least 1 week. Reduce dose with strong CYP2D6 or CYP3A4 inhibitors and in CYP2D6 poor metabolizers; increase with strong CYP3A4 inducers. Akathisia is common. Long-acting injectables are not approved for MDD.

boxedWarnings: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
approved.plainSummary: An antipsychotic added to an antidepressant when depression has not improved enough. Restlessness (akathisia) is a common side effect.

approved.indication: Adjunctive treatment to antidepressants for major depressive disorder (MDD) in adults.

dosing.notes: Titrate at weekly intervals (to 1 mg, then 2 mg). Reduce dose in moderate–severe hepatic or renal impairment, CYP2D6 poor metabolizers, and with strong CYP2D6/CYP3A4 inhibitors.

boxedWarnings: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients
approved.plainSummary: An antipsychotic added to an antidepressant for adults whose depression has not responded fully.

approved.indication: Adjunctive therapy to antidepressants for the treatment of MDD (adults with an inadequate response to antidepressant treatment).

dosing.notes: Take once daily in the evening, without food or with a light meal. Only the extended-release form carries the MDD indication; immediate-release quetiapine is not approved for MDD. Sedation, weight gain, and metabolic effects.

boxedWarnings: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
approved.plainSummary: A sedating antipsychotic, taken at night, that can be added to an antidepressant when depression has not improved enough.

approved.indication: Adjunctive therapy to antidepressants for the treatment of major depressive disorder (MDD) in adult patients.

dosing.notes: May increase to 3 mg on day 15; faster titration increased adverse reactions. Long half-life active metabolites, so effects and adverse reactions may appear weeks later. Adjust with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors; avoid with CYP3A4 inducers.

boxedWarnings: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients
approved.plainSummary: An antipsychotic capsule added to an antidepressant for adults whose depression has not responded fully.

verified.note: Contraindication (hypersensitivity) is from the known label; the contraindications section was not re-read in this pass.

approved.indication: Adjunctive therapy with antidepressants for the treatment of major depressive disorder (MDD) in adults.

dosing.notes: No titration needed. Moderate–severe hepatic impairment: 21 mg/day. Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors: 21 mg/day; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors: 10.5 mg/day; avoid CYP3A4 inducers. Approved for adjunctive MDD on November 6, 2025.

boxedWarnings: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients
approved.plainSummary: An antipsychotic taken once a day, added to an antidepressant for adults whose depression has not improved enough. It was approved for this use in late 2025.

approved.indication: Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) in adults, as monotherapy or in conjunction with an oral antidepressant.

dosing.start: 56 mg or 84 mg intranasally twice weekly (weeks 1–4)
dosing.target: 56 mg or 84 mg once weekly (weeks 5–8), then every 2 weeks or weekly
dosing.notes: Give only in a certified healthcare setting under direct supervision. Monitor for at least 2 hours after each dose, including pulse oximetry, then assess for discharge. Check BP before and about 40 minutes after dosing. No driving until the next day after a restful sleep. Assess benefit after the 4-week induction. Monotherapy use was added in January 2025.

boxedWarnings: Sedation
Dissociation
Respiratory depression
Abuse and misuse
Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients
contraindications: Aneurysmal vascular disease (thoracic/abdominal aorta, intracranial, peripheral) or arteriovenous malformation
approved.plainSummary: A nasal spray for adults whose depression has not improved after trying other antidepressants. It is given in a clinic, where patients are watched for at least 2 hours afterward.

verified.note: Checked label version 21 (revised 09/2026). TRD is defined in the trials as inadequate response to at least two antidepressants in the current episode. The current Table 1 lists 56 mg or 84 mg for the induction phase without a separate day-1 starting-dose line that older labels had; check the full label before relying on this.

approved.indication: Treatment resistant depression (major depressive disorder in patients who do not respond to 2 separate trials of different antidepressants of adequate dose and duration in the current episode).

dosing.start: 6 mg/25 mg once daily in the evening
dosing.notes: Start 3/25 or 6/25 mg in patients prone to hypotension, with hepatic impairment, or slow metabolizers. Weight gain and metabolic monitoring needed. Pediatric approval (10–17 years) is for bipolar I depression only, not TRD.

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
contraindications: Use of an MAOI within 5 weeks of stopping, or this drug within 14 days of stopping an MAOI (including linezolid or IV methylene blue)
approved.plainSummary: A capsule combining olanzapine and fluoxetine for adults whose depression has not improved after two different antidepressants. It often causes weight gain.

source.label: Olanzapine and fluoxetine capsules prescribing information (Par), DailyMed

verified.note: Drugs@FDA lists Symbyax (NDA 021520) as discontinued and its SPL could not be retrieved; generic labels (Par, Teva) are current.

approved.indication: Oral olanzapine in combination with fluoxetine for treatment resistant depression (efficacy established with Symbyax in adults). Monotherapy with either drug is not indicated for TRD.

dosing.start: Olanzapine 5 mg + fluoxetine 20 mg once daily in the evening
dosing.max: Olanzapine 18 mg + fluoxetine 75 mg (higher doses not evaluated)
dosing.notes: Adjust each component separately according to efficacy and tolerability. Same precautions as olanzapine-fluoxetine capsules.

formulations: Olanzapine tablets or orally disintegrating tablets plus fluoxetine capsules
boxedWarnings: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
contraindications: See olanzapine and fluoxetine labels (fluoxetine: MAOIs, pimozide, thioridazine)
approved.plainSummary: Taking olanzapine together with fluoxetine as separate pills is another approved option when depression has not responded to two antidepressants.

verified.note: Indication confirmed in Zyprexa (10/2026) and Prozac labels. The Zyprexa TRD dose-range text (section 2.6) was only partly read; the target range shown is from the Symbyax-based labeling and should be checked.

approved.section: Depressive symptoms with acute suicidal ideation
approved.indication: Depressive symptoms in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) with acute suicidal ideation or behavior, in conjunction with an oral antidepressant. Effectiveness in preventing suicide or reducing suicidal ideation or behavior has not been demonstrated.

dosing.target: 84 mg twice weekly for 4 weeks (may reduce to 56 mg twice weekly for tolerability)
dosing.notes: Use with an oral antidepressant. Treatment beyond 4 weeks has not been systematically evaluated. Use does not replace hospitalization when clinically warranted. Same in-clinic monitoring (at least 2 hours, pulse oximetry, BP) and REMS requirements as for TRD.

boxedWarnings: Sedation
Dissociation
Respiratory depression
Abuse and misuse
Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients
contraindications: Aneurysmal vascular disease (thoracic/abdominal aorta, intracranial, peripheral) or arteriovenous malformation
approved.plainSummary: A clinic-given nasal spray, used with an oral antidepressant, for adults with depression and current suicidal thoughts or behavior. It does not replace hospital care when needed.

verified.note: Checked label version 21 (revised 09/2026). This indication still requires an oral antidepressant; the 2025 monotherapy change applies to TRD only.

approved.indication: Prevention of seasonal major depressive episodes in patients with a diagnosis of seasonal affective disorder (SAD).

dosing.start: XL 150 mg once daily (Aplenzin 174 mg) in autumn before symptoms start
dosing.target: XL 300 mg once daily (Aplenzin 348 mg) after 1 week
dosing.notes: Start in autumn and continue through winter; the label describes tapering XL to 150 mg/day for 2 weeks before stopping in early spring. Same seizure precautions as for MDD. Only the XL (HCl) and Aplenzin (HBr) products carry this indication.

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
contraindications: Current or prior bulimia or anorexia nervosa
Abrupt discontinuation of alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or antiepileptic drugs
Use with or within 14 days of an MAOI (including linezolid or IV methylene blue)
approved.plainSummary: Once-daily bupropion started in the fall can help prevent winter depression in people with seasonal depression.

source.label: Wellbutrin XL (bupropion HCl extended-release) prescribing information, DailyMed

verified.note: Indication and starting/target doses confirmed in the Wellbutrin XL and Aplenzin labels. The SAD maximum and spring taper details were not re-read in this pass. Approval year refers to Wellbutrin XL's SAD indication.

offLabel.use: Augmentation of an antidepressant after inadequate response
offLabel.notes: A long-established augmentation strategy with the strongest evidence in older trials. Usually targeted to lower serum levels than in bipolar disorder. Requires level, renal, and thyroid monitoring. It has a narrow therapeutic index and interacts with NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and diuretics. It may also reduce suicide risk.

details.labeledFor: Lithium is FDA-approved for bipolar I disorder; not labeled as an antidepressant augmentation agent.

dosing.target: Serum level about 0.5–0.8 mEq/L (often 600–900 mg/day); lower than bipolar targets
dosing.max: Keep level at or below about 1.0 mEq/L
dosing.notes: Check level 5–7 days after changes, then renal function, calcium, and TSH every 6–12 months.

boxedWarnings: Lithium toxicity can occur at doses close to therapeutic levels
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to lithium (older labels also list significant renal or cardiovascular disease, dehydration, sodium depletion)
warnings: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, thiazides raise levels
details.plainSummary: A mood-stabilizing medicine added to an antidepressant when depression has not fully improved. Regular blood tests are needed because the safe range is narrow.

references.label: CANMAT 2023 update on clinical guidelines for management of MDD in adults (Can J Psychiatry 2024)
McQuaid et al. VA/DoD 2022 MDD guideline synopsis (Ann Intern Med 2022), PubMed
Nelson et al. Lithium augmentation meta-analysis, PubMed

offLabel.use: Augmentation of an antidepressant after inadequate response
offLabel.notes: Typically 25–50 mcg/day added to an antidepressant. In STAR*D level 3, it performed similarly to lithium with fewer discontinuations. Monitor for hyperthyroid symptoms, arrhythmia, and bone loss, especially in older adults.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for hypothyroidism and as a thyroid-suppression test aid; not for depression.

dosing.notes: Check TSH and free T4; start lower in older adults or with heart disease.

boxedWarnings: Not for obesity or weight loss; larger doses may cause serious or life-threatening toxicity
warnings: Arrhythmias and angina, especially in older adults or heart disease
Bone density loss with prolonged excess
Interacts with warfarin, digoxin, and diabetes medicines
details.plainSummary: A thyroid hormone sometimes added to an antidepressant to boost its effect. It can cause a fast heartbeat and bone thinning if the dose is too high.

references.label: CANMAT 2023 update on clinical guidelines for management of MDD in adults (Can J Psychiatry 2024)
Nierenberg et al. Lithium vs T3 augmentation after two failed medication treatments (STAR*D), PubMed

offLabel.notes: Subanesthetic IV infusions (commonly 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes) work rapidly, but effects are often short-lived without repeated dosing. Risks include dissociation, raised blood pressure, abuse potential, and limited long-term safety data. Not FDA-approved for depression (esketamine nasal spray is the approved product). Guidelines position it after multiple failed treatments.

details.labeledFor: Esketamine nasal spray (Spravato) is the FDA-approved product for treatment-resistant depression; IV racemic ketamine is approved only as an anesthetic.

dosing.target: 0.5 mg/kg twice weekly for 2–4 weeks, then individualized maintenance
dosing.max: Doses above 0.5 mg/kg are not clearly better (some clinics use up to about 1 mg/kg)
dosing.notes: Monitor blood pressure and dissociation; arrange transport home.

contraindications: Conditions where a rise in blood pressure is hazardous (aortic or intracranial aneurysm, AV malformation, recent stroke or MI)
warnings: Dissociation, anxiety, hypertension during and after the infusion
Abuse and dependence potential; bladder and liver toxicity with repeated use
Effects are often short-lived; limited long-term safety data
details.plainSummary: An anesthetic given in tiny doses through a vein for depression that has not responded to several treatments. Effects begin fast but often fade without repeat treatments.

references.label: McQuaid et al. VA/DoD 2022 MDD guideline synopsis (Ann Intern Med 2022), PubMed
CANMAT 2023 update on clinical guidelines for management of MDD in adults (Can J Psychiatry 2024)
Anand et al. Ketamine versus ECT for nonpsychotic treatment-resistant major depression (NEJM 2023), PubMed

offLabel.use: Augmentation or combination after partial response
offLabel.notes: Adding bupropion to an SSRI was comparable to buspirone augmentation in STAR*D and was a reasonable option in VA-AUGMENT/VAST-D. It may offset SSRI sexual dysfunction and fatigue. Watch for seizure risk, anxiety, and blood pressure. Bupropion inhibits CYP2D6 and can raise levels of some SSRIs (e.g., paroxetine, fluoxetine).

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for depression (IR/SR/XL), seasonal affective disorder prevention (XL), and smoking cessation (SR); combining it with an SSRI/SNRI is off-label.

dosing.target: XL 150–300 mg/day added to the SSRI/SNRI
dosing.notes: Lowers seizure threshold; raises levels of drugs cleared by CYP2D6 (paroxetine, fluoxetine).

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
contraindications: Abrupt discontinuation of alcohol or sedatives
details.plainSummary: Adding bupropion to another antidepressant can help when the first drug only partly works. It may reduce sexual side effects and low energy.

references.label: CANMAT 2023 update on clinical guidelines for management of MDD in adults (Can J Psychiatry 2024)
Trivedi et al. Medication augmentation after the failure of SSRIs (STAR*D, NEJM 2006), PubMed
Mohamed et al. Effect of antidepressant switching vs augmentation (VAST-D, JAMA 2017), PubMed

offLabel.agent: Mirtazapine (combined with an SSRI or SNRI)
offLabel.notes: Evidence is mixed. An early combination-from-the-start RCT was positive, but the larger MIR trial in primary care found no clinically meaningful benefit of adding mirtazapine to an SSRI/SNRI in treatment-resistant depression. Sedation and weight gain are common. Watch for serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for major depressive disorder as a single agent; use combined with an SSRI/SNRI is off-label.

dosing.notes: Weight gain and sedation are common.

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
details.plainSummary: Adding mirtazapine to another antidepressant can help sleep and appetite, but a large trial found little overall benefit.

references.label: Blier et al. Combination of antidepressant medications from treatment initiation (Am J Psychiatry 2010), PubMed
Kessler et al. Mirtazapine added to SSRIs or SNRIs for treatment-resistant depression (MIR trial), PubMed

offLabel.notes: Doses used in trials are higher than in Parkinson's disease, reached by slow titration (often to about 2.5 mg/day). A recent RCT in treatment-resistant depression was positive. Adverse effects include nausea, sleepiness and sudden sleep episodes, impulse-control disorders, and possible psychosis or mania.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for Parkinson's disease and restless legs syndrome; not for depression.

dosing.start: 0.125 mg at bedtime (or 0.125 mg three times daily), increased every 3–7 days
dosing.target: About 1–2.5 mg/day in the augmentation trials, reached by slow titration
dosing.notes: Reduce in renal impairment; taper rather than stop abruptly.

details.plainSummary: A Parkinson's medicine that has helped some people whose depression did not respond to usual treatments. It can cause sudden sleepiness and impulsive behaviors.

references.label: Browning et al. Pramipexole augmentation in treatment-resistant depression (PAX-D), PubMed

offLabel.use: Adjunct to an antidepressant after inadequate response
offLabel.notes: Low doses (around 0.5–3 mg/day) have positive adjunctive RCTs and are listed among adjunctive antipsychotic options in CANMAT. Not FDA-approved for MDD. Risks include hyperprolactinemia, EPS, metabolic effects, and increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for schizophrenia, bipolar I mania, and irritability in autism; not approved for MDD.

dosing.max: 3 mg/day in trials (labeled schizophrenia maximum 16 mg/day)
dosing.notes: Reassess after 4–6 weeks; check prolactin if symptoms arise.

boxedWarnings: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
warnings: Orthostasis; stroke risk in older adults with dementia
details.plainSummary: A low dose of an antipsychotic sometimes added to an antidepressant when depression has not lifted. It can cause stiffness, weight gain, and hormone changes.

references.label: CANMAT 2023 update on clinical guidelines for management of MDD in adults (Can J Psychiatry 2024)
